title: 22. Interview: DNS
summary: Interview Q&A for DNS — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 DNS interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What happens when you type a URL into the browser, focusing on DNS?
**Answer:** The browser extracts the hostname (`api.example.com`) from the URL and calls `getaddrinfo()`, which goes to the OS stub resolver. The stub checks its own cache (browsers also have their own DNS cache, separate from the OS). On a miss, the stub forwards the query to the configured recursive resolver — usually the one provided by DHCP, often `8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1`, or the ISP's resolver. The recursive resolver checks its cache; on a miss, it walks the hierarchy: queries one of the 13 root nameservers (anycast, so the nearest physical instance responds), gets a referral to the `.com` TLD nameservers; queries the TLD, gets a referral to `example.com`'s authoritative nameservers (e.g., Route 53's `ns-123.awsdns-03.com`); queries those, gets the final A record `203.0.113.42` with a TTL (say 300 seconds). The recursive resolver caches the answer for the TTL, returns it to the stub, which caches it locally. The browser then opens a TCP connection to `203.0.113.42:443` and starts the TLS handshake. The whole DNS walk is typically 4 queries (root, TLD, auth, plus the stub-to-recursive), but in practice the recursive resolver caches aggressively so most lookups hit cache.
**Visual:**
```
browser -> stub -> recursive -> root -> TLD -> authoritative -> recursive -> stub -> browser
          (libc)   (8.8.8.8)    .       .com   example.com    cache 300s     cache 300s   IP
```

### Q2. What is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative nameserver?
**Answer:** A recursive resolver (also called a caching resolver or "recursor") is the workhorse that walks the DNS hierarchy on behalf of clients. Examples include Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, the ISP's default resolver, and systemd-resolved on Linux laptops. It accepts a query from a client, checks its cache, and on a miss performs the full root → TLD → authoritative walk, caches the result for the TTL, and returns it. An authoritative nameserver, by contrast, is the source of truth for one or more zones — it answers queries only for domains it is configured to serve, and its answers are non-recursive (it either gives the answer or a referral to the next-level authoritative). Route 53, Cloudflare DNS, and BIND configured with `type master` are authoritative. The same software (BIND, PowerDNS, Knot) can run in either mode, but production deployments always separate them: a recursive resolver should never be authoritative for the domains it resolves (to avoid cache poisoning amplifying into authoritative corruption), and an authoritative server should never do recursion for arbitrary clients (to prevent DNS amplification DDoS attacks). Cloudflare runs 1.1.1.1 as a pure recursive resolver and their authoritative DNS as a separate global anycast network.
**Visual:**
```
Recursive resolver (8.8.8.8):        Authoritative (ns-123.awsdns-03.com):
  - accepts queries from clients      - answers only for zones it owns
  - walks root -> TLD -> auth         - returns A/MX/TXT records it is configured with
  - caches results for TTL            - never does recursion
  - serves many clients               - is the source of truth
  - is "the client's DNS"             - is "the domain owner's DNS"
```

### Q3. What are the common DNS record types and when would you use each?
**Answer:** The core record types: **A** maps a name to an IPv4 address (e.g., `api.example.com A 203.0.113.42`). **AAAA** maps to an IPv6 address. **CNAME** aliases one name to another (`www.example.com CNAME example.com`) — useful for pointing a subdomain at a CDN or SaaS endpoint without managing the underlying IPs, but CNAMEs cannot coexist with other records on the same name (so the apex `example.com` cannot be a CNAME, which is why Route 53 invented the proprietary ALIAS record). **MX** specifies mail exchange servers and priority (lower = higher priority). **TXT** carries arbitrary text — used for SPF (`v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all`), DKIM public keys, ACME certificate validation (`_acme-challenge.example.com TXT <token>`), and domain ownership verification. **NS** declares the authoritative nameservers for a zone. **SOA** declares zone metadata (primary NS, admin email, serial, refresh/retry/expire). **SRV** generalizes service discovery (used by Active Directory, SIP, XMPP — `_<service>._<proto>.example.com SRV 10 60 5060 sip.example.com`). **PTR** does reverse lookups (IP → name). **CAA** declares which CAs may issue certificates for the domain — critical for security after DigiNotar.
**Visual:**
```
A    api.example.com      -> 203.0.113.42        (name -> IPv4)
AAAA api.example.com      -> 2001:db8::1         (name -> IPv6)
CNAME www.example.com     -> example.com         (alias)
MX   example.com          -> 10 mail1.example.com (mail + priority)
TXT  _acme.example.com    -> "validate-xyz"      (SPF/DKIM/ACME)
NS   example.com          -> ns-123.awsdns-03.com (authoritative)
SOA  example.com          -> ns-123 hostmaster 2014030701 7200 900 1209600 86400
SRV  _sip._tcp.example.com-> 10 60 5060 sip.example.com
PTR  42.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa -> api.example.com (reverse)
CAA  example.com          -> 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
```

### Q4. Why does TTL matter, and how do you choose a TTL?
**Answer:** TTL (Time To Live) is the number of seconds a resolver is allowed to cache your record. It is the single most important DNS parameter for system designers because it directly trades off cacheability against agility. A long TTL (1 hour to 1 day) means fewer queries to your authoritative servers, lower user latency (cache hits are sub-millisecond while cache misses are 20–100 ms), and lower DNS provider cost — but a configuration mistake takes hours to recover from, because every resolver in the world holds the bad record until TTL expires. A short TTL (60 seconds) lets you reroute traffic in under a minute — essential for failover — but every resolver globally hits your authoritative servers constantly, which raises query volume 60x compared to a 1-hour TTL and may push you into a higher pricing tier on Route 53. The conventional guidance: **60–300 seconds** for production traffic that you may need to fail over (API endpoints, web frontends). **300–3600 seconds** for semi-static records. **3600–86400 seconds** for static content that changes rarely (e.g., `MX` records). For planned changes, lower the TTL 24 hours in advance, make the change, then raise it back. GitHub's 2018 outage was caused by a 24-hour TTL on a critical record — when they pushed a wrong IP, recovery took hours.
**Visual:**
```
TTL=86400 (1 day):                    TTL=60 (1 minute):
  + cached everywhere                   + cache churns every 60s
  + lowest query volume                 + fast failover (<1 min)
  + lowest user latency                 - 60x query volume vs 1-day TTL
  - 1 day to recover from bad change    - higher Route 53 bill
  - cannot fail over quickly            - more upstream latency on cold lookups

Production pattern:
  - Lower TTL to 60s 24h before planned change
  - Push change
  - Verify globally
  - Raise TTL back to 300s or 3600s
```

### Q5. What is DNSSEC and how does it work?
**Answer:** DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) adds cryptographic authentication to DNS responses, defeating cache poisoning and spoofing. It does not encrypt DNS — it just lets resolvers verify that a response genuinely came from the zone's authoritative server and was not tampered with on the wire. The mechanism: each zone has a key-signing key (KSK) and a zone-signing key (ZSK). The ZSK signs each record set; the KSK signs the ZSK; the KSK's public half is published as a DNSKEY record. To establish trust, the parent zone publishes a DS (delegation signer) record containing a hash of the child's KSK. The chain starts at the root zone's KSK, which is published as a "trust anchor" baked into every validating resolver. A recursive resolver walks the chain: root's KSK verifies root's DNSKEY, root's DS for `.com` verifies `.com`'s KSK, `.com`'s DS for `example.com` verifies `example.com`'s KSK, and `example.com`'s ZSK signs the actual A record the user asked for. If any signature fails, the resolver returns SERVFAIL instead of the (potentially poisoned) answer. Adoption is only ~5–10% of domains because key management is fragile: forgetting to roll the ZSK before expiry breaks the entire zone for validating resolvers, with no soft-fail. DNSSEC does nothing for confidentiality — DNS-over-TLS (DoT), DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), and DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ) handle that.
**Visual:**
```
Root KSK (trust anchor, in every resolver)
  |
  | signs Root DNSKEY (contains ZSK pubkey)
  v
Root ZSK signs Root's records + DS for .com
  |
  | .com DS = hash(.com KSK)
  v
.com KSK (verifiable via Root DS)
  |
  | signs .com DNSKEY + DS for example.com
  v
example.com KSK (verifiable via .com DS)
  |
  | signs example.com ZSK
  v
example.com ZSK signs: A 203.0.113.42 (RRSIG attached)

Resolver validates each signature up the chain. Any break -> SERVFAIL.
```

### Q6. What is split-horizon DNS and when would you use it?
**Answer:** Split-horizon DNS serves different answers for the same domain name depending on the source of the query. The most common pattern is internal-vs-external: inside the corporate network, `wiki.acme.com` resolves to `10.0.5.20` (the internal IP); outside, it resolves to `203.0.113.50` (the public IP behind a VPN gateway). This lets the same service name work both internally and externally without exposing internal IPs to the internet. A second pattern is geographic: Route 53's geolocation routing answers `api.acme.com` with a US-East IP for queries from North America and an EU-West IP for queries from Europe — implemented at the DNS layer. A third pattern is health-checked failover: Route 53 monitors an endpoint's health and returns the primary IP when healthy, the failover IP when not. Kubernetes uses split-horizon heavily: CoreDNS resolves `billing.svc.cluster.local` to the ClusterIP of the billing Service for in-cluster queries, while external queries for `billing.acme.com` go through an Ingress with TLS termination. The trade-off is consistency: if internal and external IPs drift, debugging becomes a "where are you asking from" problem. Always document split-horizon configs and provide tooling (`dig +short @internal-dns name` vs `dig +short @8.8.8.8 name`) for engineers to verify both views.
**Visual:**
```
            +---------------------+
            |    wiki.acme.com?   |
            +-----+---------+-----+
                  |         |
      internal    |         |   external
                  v         v
   +-----------+       +-----------+
   | internal  |       | external  |
   |  DNS view |       |  DNS view |
   +-----+-----+       +-----+-----+
         |                   |
         v                   v
   10.0.5.20            203.0.113.50
   (LAN IP)             (VPN gateway / public IP)
```

### Q7. How do DNS-based load balancing and geographic routing work?
**Answer:** DNS-based load balancing returns different IPs from a pool of backend IPs based on policy. The simplest version is round-robin: `api.example.com A 203.0.113.1` and `api.example.com A 203.0.113.2` both returned, and the resolver picks one (often the first) — clients distribute roughly evenly across the two IPs. The problem with vanilla round-robin is that resolvers cache all IPs together, so if one backend fails, clients still get the bad IP half the time. Route 53 and Cloudflare solve this with health-checked routing: they monitor each backend's health and only return healthy IPs in DNS responses. Latency-based routing (LBR) is more sophisticated: Route 53 maintains a latency table mapping source IP prefix to AWS region, and answers `api.example.com` with the IP of the lowest-latency region for the querying resolver's EDNS Client Subnet. Netflix uses LBR to route users to the closest regional fleet (US-East, EU-West, AP-Southeast). Geolocation routing is even more granular — useful for compliance ("EU users must hit EU datacenters for GDPR"). Weighted routing lets you slowly shift traffic between versions for canary deploys (5% to the new version, 95% to the old). The fundamental limit of DNS-based LB is the TTL: clients and resolvers cache for TTL seconds, so a backend that fails between DNS queries keeps getting traffic until TTL expires — which is why DNS LB is always paired with an L4/L7 load balancer in front of the actual instances.
**Visual:**
```
User in EU (via 8.8.8.8 resolver in Frankfurt):
  query: api.example.com A
  Route 53 latency-based routing -> answer: EU-West IP (50ms RTT)

User in US (via 1.1.1.1 resolver in Ashburn):
  query: api.example.com A
  Route 53 latency-based routing -> answer: US-East IP (15ms RTT)

Route 53 also health-checks each backend:
  GET https://api-eu-west.example.com/health every 30s
  if 3 consecutive failures -> remove from DNS answer pool
  TTL=60s -> recovery within 1 minute of health returning
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your company's website suddenly becomes unreachable for users in Europe but works fine for US users. Walk through your debugging.
**Answer:** Start by reproducing the issue from a European vantage point — use a tool like `dig` from a European shell, or a public DNS debugging service like DNSChecker.org that queries from ~100 global locations. If `dig` from EU returns an empty or wrong answer while US returns the expected IP, the problem is in DNS, not the application. Check three layers in order. (1) **Authoritative**: query your authoritative nameservers directly (`dig @ns-123.awsdns-03.com api.example.com`) from EU and US. If they differ, you have a split-horizon or geolocation routing misconfiguration. If EU is being routed to a US-East IP when it should be EU-West, your Route 53 latency-based or geolocation policy is wrong. (2) **Recursive resolvers**: query `dig api.example.com @8.8.8.8` from EU. If the recursive resolver returns a stale or wrong answer while authoritative returns the right one, the issue is TTL caching of a previous bad config — you need to wait for TTL to expire or lower the TTL proactively before pushing changes. (3) **DNSSEC**: if you recently rolled keys and EU resolvers are validating (8.8.8.8 validates, some ISPs don't), a broken RRSIG would cause SERVFAIL specifically on validating resolvers. Check `dig +dnssec api.example.com` and look for `ad` (authenticated data) flag. The most common cause I have seen in practice: a Route 53 geolocation record was created for "Europe" but the routing policy was accidentally set to "weighted" with 0% weight on the EU record.
**Visual:**
```
Debugging ladder:
  1. dig @8.8.8.8 api.example.com        (recursive view from EU)
  2. dig @ns-123.awsdns-03.com api.example.com  (authoritative direct)
  3. dig +dnssec api.example.com         (DNSSEC validation)
  4. DNSChecker.org from 100 sites       (global propagation view)
  5. Route 53 console: check geo/latency policy, health checks, TTL
```

### Q2. You need to migrate your domain's authoritative DNS from one provider to another with zero downtime. How?
**Answer:** The safe migration sequence has six steps. (1) Lower the TTL on the current NS records at the registrar from 172800 seconds (the default 48 hours for NS records) to 300 seconds, at least 48 hours before the migration — this lets resolvers pick up the new NS records quickly once you change them. (2) Replicate the entire zone into the new provider (export BIND zone file, import into Route 53 / Cloudflare). (3) Verify the new provider returns identical answers to the old one for every record type — A, AAAA, MX, TXT, CNAME, NS, SOA, CAA, SRV. Run a script that diffs the two responses for every record. (4) At the registrar, update the NS delegation to point to the new provider's nameservers. (5) Monitor DNS query volume at the old provider — it should taper off over the next 48 hours as resolvers expire their caches and pick up the new NS records. Keep the old provider running for at least 1 week past the last query, to absorb any stragglers. (6) After the old provider sees zero queries for a week, decommission it. The critical pitfall: do not change any IP records during the migration window — the new provider must serve the same IPs as the old one. If you also need to change IPs, do that as a separate step after the NS migration is fully propagated. GitHub and Heroku have both had multi-hour outages from botched DNS migrations where they changed NS and IPs simultaneously.
**Visual:**
```
T-48h: lower NS TTL 172800 -> 300
T-24h: replicate zone to new provider, verify diffs = 0
T-0:   update NS at registrar to new provider's NS
T+0..48h: monitor query volume at old provider (should taper)
T+7d:  if old provider sees 0 queries for 7 days, decommission
(separate step: change A records AFTER NS migration complete)
```

### Q3. You are designing a multi-region active-active API. How do you use DNS to route users to the closest healthy region?
**Answer:** Use Route 53 latency-based routing (LBR) with health-checked records. Create one record per region: `api.example.com A 203.0.113.1` (US-East, latency policy), `api.example.com A 198.51.100.1` (EU-West, latency policy), `api.example.com A 192.0.2.1` (AP-Southeast, latency policy). Route 53 maintains a global latency table mapping source IP prefix to AWS region, and answers each query with the IP of the lowest-latency region for the querying resolver's EDNS Client Subnet. Attach a Route 53 health check to each record (GET `https://api-us-east.example.com/health` every 30 seconds, 3 consecutive failures = unhealthy). When a region's health check fails, Route 53 omits that region's IP from the answer, and clients fall back to the next-lowest-latency healthy region. Set the TTL to 60 seconds so failover completes within a minute. Critical detail: many users behind corporate networks use centralized DNS resolvers (e.g., a German office using `8.8.8.8` resolving from a Frankfurt PoP) — without EDNS Client Subnet (ECS), Route 53 sees the resolver's location, not the user's, and may route a German user to US-East. Enable ECS on your authoritative provider and ensure your recursive resolvers support it (8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1 do; some ISP resolvers don't). Always pair DNS-based routing with an L7 load balancer in each region for finer-grained health checking and traffic splitting.
**Visual:**
```
api.example.com (Route 53 latency-based routing, TTL=60)
  |- US-East IP    (health-checked, returns when healthy)
  |- EU-West IP    (health-checked, returns when healthy)
  |- AP-Southeast  (health-checked, returns when healthy)

User in Berlin via 1.1.1.1 (supports ECS, Frankfurt PoP):
  -> Route 53 sees EDNS Client Subnet = German IP prefix
  -> answers with EU-West IP
  -> failover: if EU-West health check fails, returns US-East (next closest)
```

### Q4. Your CDN tells you to set a CNAME from `www.example.com` to `example.com.cdn.net`, but your apex domain `example.com` also needs to point at the CDN. CNAME at the apex is forbidden by RFC. What do you do?
**Answer:** You are hitting the classic apex-CNAME problem. RFC 1033 forbids CNAME coexisting with any other record type on the same name, but the apex must have SOA and NS records (otherwise the zone is broken). So you cannot put a CNAME at `example.com`. Solutions: (1) **ALIAS record (Route 53 proprietary)** — Route 53 internally resolves the CNAME target at query time and returns an A record, so the client sees an A record while you configure it as an alias to a CDN endpoint. This is the cleanest solution if you are on Route 53. (2) **CNAME flattening (Cloudflare, NS1, DNSimple)** — same idea, the provider flattens the CNAME chain at query time and returns the final A record. (3) **Use a www-only domain** — set `www.example.com CNAME example.com.cdn.net`, redirect `example.com` to `www.example.com` at the HTTP layer (301 redirect from a small origin server). (4) **ALTERNATE: do not CNAME at all** — point `example.com A` directly at the CDN's anycast IPs. Most CDNs publish a list of static IPs you can use; the downside is you lose the CDN's DNS-based routing, because the CDN needs to see the query to pick the closest PoP. For modern deployments on AWS, option 1 with Route 53 ALIAS to CloudFront is the standard pattern — it gives you both apex support and the CDN's geographic routing.
**Visual:**
```
Forbidden:                              Working (Route 53 ALIAS):
  example.com  CNAME example.cdn.net      example.com  ALIAS d1.cloudfront.net
  example.com  SOA  ...                   example.com  SOA  ...
  example.com  NS   ...                   example.com  NS   ...
  --> RFC violation                       --> Route 53 resolves d1.cloudfront.net
      (SOA/NS + CNAME coexist)                at query time, returns A record
                                              (CDN still sees the query for routing)
```

### Q5. Your company has been the victim of DNS spoofing attacks. What defenses do you deploy?
**Answer:** Layer four defenses. (1) **DNSSEC signing** on your authoritative zones — sign all record sets with RRSIG, publish DNSKEY, and have your parent zone publish DS records so resolvers can validate the chain. This makes spoofing cryptographically detectable. (2) **Use a managed authoritative provider with built-in anti-spoofing** — Route 53, Cloudflare, NS1 all randomize source ports and TXIDs to make spoofing harder (Kaminsky attack relies on predictable TXID/port). (3) **Deploy DNS-over-TLS / DNS-over-HTTPS** on your recursive resolvers — this encrypts the stub-to-recursive channel, defeating on-path spoofing. (4) **Run a validating recursive resolver** that checks DNSSEC signatures — if a spoofed response has no valid RRSIG, the resolver returns SERVFAIL rather than the poisoned answer. (5) **HSTS preloading** on your web endpoints — even if a user's DNS is spoofed to a malicious IP, the browser refuses to connect without a valid cert for your domain, which the attacker cannot obtain. (6) **CAA records** restricting which CAs can issue certs for your domain — so even an attacker who obtains a fraudulent cert from a misbehaving CA cannot use it against your domain. (7) **Monitor Certificate Transparency logs** for unauthorized cert issuance. (8) **Short TTLs** so any successful poisoning self-heals quickly. The Kaminsky vulnerability of 2008 is the canonical case study; DNSSEC was the long-term fix, but adoption has been slow.
**Visual:**
```
Spoofing attack (no DNSSEC):
  attacker on path injects: api.example.com A 6.6.6.6 (fake)
  resolver caches it for TTL -> users go to attacker IP

With DNSSEC:
  attacker injects fake A record
  resolver checks RRSIG against DNSKEY chain
  signature does NOT verify -> SERVFAIL returned
  users see error, not attacker IP
  (does not fix availability, but does fix integrity)

Layered defense: DNSSEC + DoT/DoH + HSTS preload + CAA + CT monitoring
```

### Q6. You are launching a new feature that should be visible to 5% of users for canary testing. How do you use DNS for traffic splitting?
**Answer:** Route 53 weighted routing is the standard answer. Create two records with the same name: `api.example.com A 203.0.113.1` (the existing version) with weight 95, and `api.example.com A 198.51.100.1` (the new canary version) with weight 5. Route 53 returns each IP proportional to its weight, so ~5% of queries get the canary IP. Set TTL to 60 seconds so you can adjust the weights and have traffic shift within a minute. Critical caveats: (1) DNS-based splitting is per-query, not per-user — once a user's resolver caches the canary IP, that user keeps hitting the canary until TTL expires. This is usually fine, but if you need per-user sticky canary assignment, use a cookie-based canary at the L7 layer instead. (2) Many users behind a corporate NAT share a single recursive resolver, so all of them get the same answer — your 5% may be lumpy. (3) EDNS Client Subnet helps — Route 53 sees the user's subnet and can vary the answer accordingly. (4) Health checks still apply — if the canary backend fails its health check, Route 53 omits it and 100% goes to the existing version. For higher-fidelity canaries, the modern pattern is to use a service mesh (Istio) with HTTP-header-based traffic splitting at the L7 layer, which gives per-request (not per-resolver) granularity. Netflix's Spinnaker canary stage typically uses DNS for initial low-percentage canaries and switches to L7 for fine-grained ramp.
**Visual:**
```
api.example.com (Route 53 weighted, TTL=60)
  |- weight 95  -> 203.0.113.1 (existing v1)
  |- weight  5  -> 198.51.100.1 (canary v2)

~5% of queries return canary IP
~95% of queries return existing IP

Ramp-up sequence: 5% -> 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 95% -> 100%
(adjust weights, wait 60s+TTL, monitor metrics, repeat)
```

### Q7. Your startup's DNS is currently served by a single BIND server in your office. How do you make it production-grade?
**Answer:** Single-server DNS is a single point of failure for your entire business — if that BIND goes down, every service disappears from the internet in TTL seconds. The migration has several layers. (1) **Move authoritative DNS to a managed anycast provider** — Route 53, Cloudflare DNS, NS1, or Akamai. These run global anycast networks with hundreds of PoPs, so the nearest instance responds to each resolver. (2) **Run at least 4 authoritative nameservers across at least 2 providers** — Route 53 + Cloudflare, for example, so a single provider outage does not take you down. (3) **Set TTL to 60–300 seconds** for production endpoints so you can fail over quickly. (4) **Enable DNSSEC** on the zone — sign with KSK/ZSK, publish DS at the parent, use a key management process that rolls keys before expiry. (5) **Use health-checked records** — Route 53 health-checks each backend and removes unhealthy IPs from answers. (6) **Add CAA records** restricting which CAs can issue certificates. (7) **Monitor DNS as a Tier-1 dependency** — alert if authoritative query latency spikes, if health-check-fail rate rises, or if query volume drops (which may indicate resolver caching issues). (8) **Have a DNS incident runbook** — know how to lower TTLs, push emergency changes, and fail over between providers. (9) **Document split-horizon configs** explicitly. The BIND-in-the-office pattern is fine for a hobby project; in production it is a business-ending single point of failure. Companies like GitHub and Slack have all moved to multi-provider anycast DNS precisely because they learned this the hard way.
**Visual:**
```
Before (fragile):              After (production-grade):
  +----------------+            Route 53 (anycast, 60+ PoPs)   |
  | BIND in office |            + Cloudflare DNS (anycast)     | >= 2 providers
  | single server  |            + health-checked records       | anycast
  | no failover    |            + TTL 60-300s                  | DNSSEC
  +----------------+            + DNSSEC signed                | CAA records
         |                     + CAA records                  | monitoring
         v                     + runbook + multi-provider
   single point of failure      + split-horizon documented
```

quiz.explanation: DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) adds cryptographic authentication to DNS responses, defeating cache poisoning and spoofing. It does not encrypt DNS — it just lets resolvers verify that a response genuinely came from the zone's authoritative server and was not tampered with on the wire. The mechanism: each zone has a key-signing key (KSK) and a zone-signing key (ZSK).
